english: They had these things from the great God.

So that I may also use a human example, I say, that the grammarian writes grammatically; but not always every writer has it correctly from grammar, but also from luck and habit. It appears therefore according to greatness, that he who is great alone, by doing, does great things; and analogously also according to our power we contemplate God and receive the concept of God Himself.

And he said this so that the friends, those supposing a single cause of labors, might understand that he who does great and fearsome and deep judgments has them also unsearchable, which are also glorious, as to say filled with glory. Paul also writes something similar, saying: 'O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God; how unsearchable are his judgments and unsearchable are his ways; for who has known the mind of the Lord?' (Rom 11:33). And in the Psalms there is something near: 'Great are your judgments' (Ps 18:49). For who having understood heaven, sun, moon, stars, and the motions of these, will not marvel at the Creator? And if even you were to pass through into each thing even to the smallest of him, as that teaches: 'Go to the ant, you sluggard' (Prov 6:6) and the following, you will marvel at the wisdom of this God. If he surpasses me, I shall not see, and if he passes me by, I have not even known how.

The ungraspable nature of God's judgments is signified here; for for man, and more so by nature born, to grasp these things by private effort is impossible. This [is]... to him... this the holy [one]... came to the mind, so that from the inability to grasp the judgments of God they might understand and remember Him, and [understand] regarding the things happening to Him as not being accidental, and so that they might avoid supposing a single cause regarding the things happening. Whether therefore or whether therefore, he says, whether the Lord surpasses me or passes me by, so that he is even near to me, I am not able to know by...

of my mind regarding what becomes men. For someone wishing something might elude him, and surpassing him and passing by, will not sufficiently grasp it. And it is possible even to say, that if the things concerning the earth were to become near to me, I would be able to know according to our imposition; for how the economy of the heaven and those in it happens is unknown to me; if indeed I should come again to the lands, God passing by me and in some way training me among them, even so I am not self-sufficient in knowing.

If he removes [it], who will turn back? Or who will say to him: 'What have you done?'; for he himself has turned away in anger. To remove is possible in every matter upon which God works; for if he wished to dissolve human life, who can turn back his will? If to bring about painful things or to cease these, no one of those things happening from him can promise a hindrance, nor can anyone of strength say to him: 'What have you done?'; according to the apostolic word: 'Shall not the creature say to the creator: Why have you made me thus?' (Romans 9:20). ... let those speaking blasphemously to him say: 'What have you done?'; for not ... the word, but ... of him worthy of ... 'What have you done?'; for those calculating the bitter things for a short time, not knowing their purpose, speak blasphemously: 'What have you done?'; according to the fool saying in his own heart: 'There is no God.' And he also brings the reason for not being able to say anything to him: 'What have you done?'; asserting: 'For he himself has turned away in anger'; for by a judgment of anger he has made the turning away. But someone, recognizing this graciously, said: 'I will bear the anger of the Lord, because I have sinned against him' (Psalm 38:18). Therefore he turns away the worthy in anger; but the righteous one does not have the worth of anger, so he has not turned away the righteous. Even if the righteous one suffers, it is not by anger, but he undergoes a struggle. For look, if one is being disciplined as a combatant, and another is being struck, is not the same manner of wounds? Thus even painful things to the righteous and...

english: When a bad thing happens, it did not occur in the same way; for one is under wrath, the bad one, I say, but the other did not, but rather turned away the wrath from the righteous, desiring to prove himself a victor, as the witnesses and Job himself. For he turned away the wrath being sent upon the bad ones by making his virtue manifest. And the cattle under heaven were scorched by him.

And according to the account of history this is true; for if he himself had not subjected them, these things would have been beyond doubt to men. And even in the other predatory beasts you will find this by passing through the reasoning. But also the evil spirits, the cattle named allegorically, he himself bent. For neither was human nature such that it would not be scorched by God without being so. And it is fitting that he also spoke of those under heaven, in order to make all things manifest, those in the air and in the earth and in the lower regions. For all things have been subjected: 'for the cattle was spread by knowledge' (Job 39:25).

And if God had not said so continually, not even to Job: 'the beginning of evil is the devil' (Job 1:6). For the opposing powers do not come by their own wicked intention. For they do not have authority to approach with evil and hardship, unless God permits it. But they hasten to cast evil by their own impulse. For so also, according to a private intention, 'into the heart of Judas' (Luke 22:3) those providing him with sufferings, they gather evils dwelling there.

If he obeys me, does he discern my words? He wishes to teach that not, if we pray for something, this does not always happen 'and' in agreement with our words for the discernment of God. 'For what we ought to pray for according to what is necessary, we do not know.' What therefore he says is such: that even if he obeys, he does not discern human words to approve them in this way, but his own judgment, being wise, will impose it upon us, being a lover of mankind and doing nothing unjustly. For if, O righteous one, he does not listen to me, I will entreat his judgment. He confirms what was said before, teaching that even if someone is perfect among men, the eye of God 'searches the things of the heart' (Romans 7:24) and perceives even the unseen. Such is what the apostle says: 'I know nothing about myself, but I am not acquitted by this; but the one who judges me is the Lord' (1 Cor 4:3); therefore the saint desires his judgment according to: 'refine the...'

"the kidneys and my heart," which no one in a state of sinning says. Still, regarding these things, he teaches them again not to grasp the secondary things for a single cause, by assuming a hypothesis: that if anyone is righteous and prays for pleasant things hypothetically, he will not certainly be heard; for even he requires the judgment of God.

There are some who have read the verse without a substantiation, that it is: "He will not listen to my righteousness" (Job 11:6). Understand then, that the repayment has a reason, because the one who spoke before, the friend, was saying: "But you rise up early to the Lord praying; if you are good and true, he will listen to the prayer of supplication" (Job 8:6), teaching him that God does not always give to us the words we ask, but those that are profitable; he says this hypothetically, that "for if you are righteous, he will not listen to me;" for thus the judgment triumphs.

He spoke hypothetically because even the holy one knows that the judgment must persuade him and not demand a solution from him unseasonably. Even if I call and he obeys, I do not believe that he has listened to me, lest he should turn me away through my ignorance. Since it was easy and convenient for Bildad to say to the blessed Job, as we also said before, the "but you rise up early" and the following, toward his own words spoken without distinction, teaching that the one praying will not certainly succeed, nor is it fitting to ask God for everything with "uncovering hands"; for he who sends up prayer rightly to God deserves to receive those things which are effective for him and suit the one bestowing.

english: These things apply to both kings and commoners. It seems he also stirs them up so that they do not think that they have been separated from their equals because of the duties they are surrounded by; for these things are common to the important and the trivial, to the free and the slave, to the commoner and the ruler, and quite simply to all.

But the things sent upon them because of triviality, he has made a separation for the sinners from all the righteous. For 'the death of the righteous is precious before the Lord' (Ps 116:15). And concerning the trivial, it is said: 'the death of sinners is bitter' (Prov 1:32). And the dissolution of the soul from the body is the same; but the trivial one receives punishment, because his death is shameful, while the important one receives promise and divine rewards; for 'the Lord takes' 'the gentle' (Ps 103:13). And to each of the righteous is a similar voice, by which they say: 'He who raises me from the gates of death' (Ps 18:4). Of what death, indeed, is this, or the one that consumes the soul from blessed life? For this one, having been raised from the gates of death, comes to the gates of blessed life beyond, bringing forth: 'that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion' (Ps 78:7). These are indeed excellent deeds and entries into good works.

But the righteous are mocked and are delivered into the hands of the ungodly. The trivial ones, he says, truly experience in death what is shameful, but the righteous are mocked by the trivial ones doing this, when they see them being in distress. This is not a reproach of the righteous, but of those who mock, not knowing that they are being delivered into the hands of the ungodly; which he says he is making manifest, thus showing the cause of his own ill-treatment. For it was not fitting then to say, that because of a struggle I am delivered into the hands of the ungodly and such a trial is; for sometimes, as if being self-exalting, he gave space to the adversary to seize him. He will cover the faces of his judges. He shows the harshness of the ungodly by covering his faces to approach deceitfully to deceive. It is therefore said: 'Who shall uncover his face-covering, or who shall enter to fold his garment?' (Job 13:13). english: He did not recognize the evil. Understand, then, that even a third level of thought can be expressed by another orator established in Amos, the second of the twelve prophets. Concerning those who squander and are lovers of pleasure, and who rejoice in this very thing in the delights of life, he says: 'Those sleeping on ivory beds, those squandering upon their couches, those shouting at the sounds of instruments and anointing themselves with the first myrrh, those drinking filtered wine, they considered it as standing [permanent], not as fleeing.'

For they judged the delights of life to be adjacent, present, and continuous. Therefore he says that those marveling at well-being, such as being healthy, being rich, or reaching [heights], do not consider that these things are being distributed in such a way that they do not know them, just as it is impossible to recognize a path when the sea is surging, or an eagle flying swiftly because it seeks prey. In truth, the passage of delights and human things is rapid, as can be learned from what was said concerning wealth by the Psalmist: 'Do not fear when a man prospers and when the glory of his house increases, for he shall not take all things in his dying, nor shall the glory of his house descend with him' (Psalm 49:16-17).

If I say, 'I will take pains in speaking, bowing my face and sighing,' a mark of magnanimity is shown in these things. For he says that even if, having received a concept of those things which are unpleasant, I say something about them, I immediately forget them, not being enslaved by them, but occupying myself with the contemplation of virtue. Similar to this is what is said by David, that 'I forgot to eat my bread' (Psalm 63:11). For the memory of divine and heavenly things brings forgetfulness to those who are being overwhelmed by them. And if, he says, I also sigh, doing this while bowing my face, through which in a certain way he shows his worship toward God; and even if he says this, he performs the painful things toward his own heart...

They are found in a good state according to the blessed Paul: 'troubled in all things, but not in distress; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed' (2 Cor 4:8). I shake with all my limbs. This is evident, according to the sense, that they understand. For no limb of his was found healthy; for 'from feet' even 'to head' he was struck (Job 7:4).

And if you say that all his limbs had a familiarity toward him, who were also shaken in such a way as to either leave him or in some way attempt to distance themselves, as if he suffers these things because of sin, consider this. For I know that you will not declare me innocent. The moderation of the saint is known through this, and a great gratitude. For he says, that becoming my examiner, being precise—for you are God—you will not declare me innocent.

For even if he said, 'I know that I will appear righteous,' yet he knew and is persuaded that, as a tester before God, 'there is no star pure in his sight' (Ps 8:3) and he himself makes it clear. Such is what the blessed Paul says, writing: 'I do not know myself' (1 Cor 4:6). Then, not giving [credit] to himself, he proceeds: 'but not in this am I justified, but He who judges me is the Lord' (1 Cor 4:4).

And this saint also clearly knows the weakness of human nature, saying: 'exceedingly we were burdened beyond strength, so that we were driven to despair, even of life. But we ourselves have received in ourselves the sentence of death, so that we might not trust in ourselves, but in God.' And even if the saints suffer in their afflictions, they have within themselves the sentence, so that they may give the trust to God and not to themselves; as this same blessed one says: I know that my being innocent is not from myself, not with you cooperating, just as the wise Paul says, 'not I, but the grace with me' (2 Cor 12:9), and the holy David: 'I was troubled and I did not speak' (Ps 39:9). Since I am impious, why did I not die?

english: He moves to the assumption regarding friends. For since it is assumed that those sinning follow the evil-doers to fall into bad circumstances, and that dying is worse for all according to life-lovers, he asks them: 'Since I am impious according to you, why did I not die?' In order that in the question he might provide them with an understanding, that there is some other cause bringing about the secondary things. And he does the same in other matters, asking again: 'Why do the impious live, having been prospered even in wealth, their seed according to the soul, and their cattle not having failed to calve?' In order that he might also instruct through these, he seeks the existing causes from God of the things happening to men, which are secondary and pleasant. For many times the wicked have remained in what are considered prosperities, as Solomon said of them, that—as even the blessed Job says, that 'even in the sleep of Hades they rested' (Job 3:13). For if I should wash myself with snow and cleanse myself with clean hands, you have sufficiently dyed me in filth, and my clothing has become loathsome to me. Again, so that we might not think him a deceiver, he says these things, that even if I exist purely in such a way, as through manifest deeds, which he named hands, cleansing myself, I have again filth; concerning which it is to be sought, comparing the similar to the spoken: 'No one is clean from filth, nor even for one hour is his life upon the earth.' And 'the mind of men is carefully set upon evil from youth' (Psalm 143:10), which shows the character that is youthful, just as it was said to someone not to receive a new listener. These things, then, trouble those who have nothing set upon this life; for how is the one now formed not unclean? And it must be understood sensibly that the sin of succession according to Adam is to be taken, which is brought forward by them incoherently. For even the saints, even if they have not come into life for the sake of anything else, have the filth in childhood age, which is not sin. According to this it was said concerning Samuel: 'And Samuel before knowing God' (1 Samuel 3:7). And the child was not knowing God, not because of malice, but because he had not the knowledge of the word. And you will sensibly understand 'all have sinned' (Romans 3:23) if you take those according to ignorance, those according to childhood age. And let it be by example: one being at the hundredth degree reaching the hundredth, if he descends three, one would say he is seeing [the one] beginning from...

The one who went from the first to the third is not being reproached. He who submitted the hundred, even if he did not depart from the ranks, is indeed in some filth. For Job says that even if he is pure, he has filth, and not a small filth, but something like a dye.

For it is not only through sin that one comes into this life, but also through the benefit of others, as one carries John or Jeremiah; therefore he says that even if he is pure through his deeds, he still has filth. For filth, in relation to pure life, is not the earthly place itself, but as it is said: 'All our righteousness is as a filthy garment before you, Lord' (Isa 64:6). Which the Lord washes according to what is said in Isaiah: 'The Lord will wash the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst' (Isa 1:16). Filth, then, might be the unintentional things, but blood is that which is done by intention.

By what is he washed? Either 'by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning,' the spirit of judgment revealing discernment and the spirit of burning revealing punishment? Both work a correction. Because of this, he says, 'she has loathed me, my garment,' alluding to the weight of the stay here; which is also shown by 'hating even the tunic defiled by the flesh,' which is the mixing with those from among humans. He says, therefore, that she hated the human intercourse which he had.

That the garment signifies the state is clear from what was said to the prodigal by the father: 'Bring out his first garment' (Luke 15:22). And that the blood signifies sin is evident from what was said to the devil: 'In what way a garment stained in blood will not be clean, so also you will not be clean.' Through being stained in blood, the magnitude of the evil is shown. The blessed one should not be surprised that he says one thing toward friends and another toward God. For he encountered opposition when, speaking to the same person, he confessed himself both righteous and a sinner. Therefore, toward God, with moderation, he says he is stained with filth in relation to His own purity, but toward men he converses differently, saying: 'I know that I shall appear righteous.' That the saints use such a kind of speech can also be learned from the letters of Paul.

english: Saying 'seven flaxen lines', the saints, having endured much, suffer in soul under the opposing power, indeed as participating in human nature, but they do not fall from the divine purpose. And David, having become in such a war, sings: 'I was troubled and I did not speak' (Psalm 43:5); and again: 'Why are you dejected, my soul, and why are you disturbed within me?' (Psalm 42:5); and just as his own intellect is being shaken, he approaches with exhortation saying: 'Hope in God, for I shall confess to Him' (Psalm 42:5). Thus also the blessed Job says with gratitude, making manifest to God the sincerity of his intellect: 'For he is not a man according to me, against whom I am judged' (Job 13:15).

The word is thus being smoothed out without following: 'I myself know the things concerning myself. And since the friends, not being moved by right reasoning, and from the distressing ones standing around, think that I have suffered through sin, I am satisfied with Your testing.' Then, through them, in a certain way teaching them again, that the things concerning him are not human, he says: 'He is not a man according to me, against whom I am judged,' as knowing all things concerning him and therefore bearing it, so that the friends might imitate him, considering that the word according to him is a secret, and thus they turn away from the single delusion, so that we may come together in judgment.

As has been said, he teaches the friends to perceive that the conscience is well-situated and ready for judgment; for the conscience does not wish to come to judgment with itself. He says these things not losing boldness toward God, testifying with Him concerning righteousness, but in order to teach, as has been said, the friends that he is not afraid of reproof. For he did not have anything worthy of reproof. David, participating in this boldness, sang: 'My heart is prepared, O God, my heart is prepared' (Psalm 57:7). Would that He were our Mediator, who reproves and discerns in the midst of both. Again, these things are said in a general way, in the manner in which the first things were said, being the clearest evidence of the freedom of his soul. He prays, therefore, that there might exist some examination which demonstrates to the friends that he suffers these things not because of sin, but for the sake of a struggle. And the saint intended these things, not boasting, but first indeed, in order to...

Friends should have correct views regarding these matters, so that they do not sin against God by falling away, which happens often when they do not find or realize the sin within themselves or in others. Since the title of the Mediator is now at issue, it is worthy to understand how the Savior is called 'a mediator of God and men'. Man, therefore—and what am I saying, man—is far removed from the creature of the Creator.

You find in the nature of things that when much is separated into the same, it possesses a middle element. Just as for a simple example the shell of a nut is hard and the food is watery, there lies between us something stronger than the shell and drier than the liquid, and thus they are joined; this is also seen in nuts and in streams. Since God has separated man greatly, the Son, being consubstantial with God, possessed the human in himself, so that by the familiarity toward men and the consubstantiality toward God he might join both sides and 'break the middle wall of the partition, the enmity, in his flesh' (Ephesians 2:14), assuming the rank of a high priest.

And the high priest is a middle between God and the consecrated ones, bringing the things of God to men and the things of men to God; he offers prayers and supplications to God as sacrifices, and provides the knowledge of Him to men. He sends up a prayer, saying: 'just as I and you are one, so that these also may be one in us.' Then this will be, when God becomes 'all in all' (1 Corinthians 15:28), so that the rest may be joined to God without a mediator, becoming one spirit with Him.

For the blessed Job also foresaw this Mediator with divine sight, which is clear from 'he who is about to grasp a great beast' (Job 42:2) and from 'he who walks as if on land upon the sea' (Job 9:8). For when God was being revealed to him, there was no room for doubt that he was fully informed concerning the economy. 'Remove the rod from me, and let his terror not turn me aside' (Job 42:21). The severe discipline is signified by the name of the rod, and especially in rebuke when it is spoken. english: "...their lawlessness." For this rebuke and all that is from God does not harm the one being rebuked, but instructs him. And that it is thus, Paul writes to the Corinthians: "What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love?" (1 Cor 4:21), which is to say: Shall I approach as a beloved, or as required for correction? For a certain way of the one being corrected by oppressors seems to suggest that he does not love him. A wise saying has also been said regarding the rod: "For he who brings wisdom from his lips strikes a heartless man with a rod" (Prov 13:24), calling the rebuke and the corrective word a rod. Since this is useful, the divine word presents it, saying: "He who spares his rod hates his own son" (Prov 13:24), even though according to men, one might be thought to love by not striking the son.

Therefore, he wants to be freed from this, not out of brevity, but so that they may be instructed, setting another cause for their labors, so that he does not endure these things because of sin. "And I will not be afraid, but I will speak." For I do not thus persist, the soul weary. Groaning, I will lay my words upon him. I will speak, being seized by bitterness of soul. He wants to instruct them, not to have the burden or to impose labors, but to understand that even while existing in tribulations, he answers with a strengthened mind. He says, therefore, that if the mediator had been freed from the oppressors—what you think was laid upon me because of sin—if, having been enslaved to you, I had been freed from them, I would have spoken without fear; and he says, measuring [his words], "I cannot think thus, being weary from the labors." But if, as you say, it was because of sin, I would have spoken groaning and, being seized by bitterness, I would have spoken to prove the purity of my conscience, demonstrating it. And I would say to the Lord, "Teach me not to be impious, and why did you judge me thus?" I would have said to the Lord, if the only cause against you was the punishment through sin: "Teach me not to be impious." For if even one not sinning is punished because of sin, then to sin would be more preferable. Otherwise, one who is not such is taught to sin, if there is only one cause for suffering. And I would have also said, "Why did you judge me thus," to "He who knows the hearts," unless it were understood that because of the excuse...

Having received these things, I remain. He says these things by powerfully casting upon them a desire for inquiry, so that the answer concerning his purity might seem to come from their own prompting and not from himself, which seemed to be arrogant. 'Is it good for you, if I speak unjustly, that I spoke of your works of hands?' And he would have said this, if, as you behave, the temptations were through sin: 'Is it good for you, if I speak unjustly, that I spoke of nothing sinning, [as] being a work of your hands?' For if the diligent man is punished for a fault just as the wicked man is, the occasion is superfluous according to you. But pay attention to the counsel of the ungodly.

Or, as a mortal sees repeatedly, 'either' your life is human 'or' your years are of a man. It is possible to say of him that he pays attention to the one asking, casting down the truth, that he does not suffer according to the preceding word—I say, through sin. And it is possible also to count these toward the counsel of the ungodly; for they do not say pious things, having seized the evils in a single way, that everyone being afflicted through sin is afflicted. I would have also said the 'as a mortal sees repeatedly,' if, as you behave, there were one cause of the afflictions, and 'your life is human or your years are of a man.'

I would have said all these things if I had encountered the same opinion of you; but knowing that there is not one cause of the temptations, but also occurring through struggle, I know that God is not merely observing the phenomena as a man does, but is stepping into the depth of the soul, thus testing each one justly. It should be noted, as also elsewhere, that 'life' (bios) is a very significant name. For it signifies wealth, as it is said in the Song of Songs: 'If a man gives his whole life in love, they will nullify him.' And it also signifies the life that exists, as if John says: 'But whoever has the life of the world and sees his brother in need and closes his bowels against him.' And both the right conduct and the bad are called 'life,' as if we say: he has a practical life, or that the other has a bad life. Here, however, he spoke of the life of a man as a sojourner in this age. He says, therefore, that if you had such a life—instead of a time being described—as a man, I would have distinguished [you] as being toward one who is ignorant. But God...

english: It is eternal; for it is said, 'For you are the same, and your years will not fail' (Job 14:5). And again, 'In generation of generations the years' (Job 14:18). The existence of God is uncircumscribable, for He is eternal. Therefore, Job would say, 'You know nothing of what is concerning me,' meaning, 'You have searched out my iniquity and traced my sins.'

He says this while reproaching them again, that the calamity concerning me is the result of many having sinned. Since the friends reckoned him as suffering through sin, he shows them abruptly that it is not so, by saying, 'O God, your years are not like a man's, for you have searched out my iniquity' (Job 9:33). For according to these words, he suggests that you do not punish me as a sinner, and you do not seek out our iniquity or sin through inductions against those disposed in this way.

'For you know that I have not been impious' (Job 27:5). He reveals the knowledge of the matter to them by saying to God, 'You know that I have not been impious.' But these friends think that the things coming upon me have been brought about because of an impious man. But who is the one being taken out from your hands? He again suggests the idea that it is possible for one who has not sinned to fall into afflictions; for God knows that Job did not act impiously.

And the question, 'But who is the one being taken out from your hands?' brings on the instruction of the friends, showing that the one who has not sinned and has not acted impiously comes under the hand of God into afflictions through struggle and the demonstration of endurance. For those who are afflicted, yet do not fall because of the tribulations, say, 'In all things being afflicted, but not in anguish' (2 Cor 4:8). And again it is said, 'Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and out of all of them He will rescue them' (Ps 34:19).

But to be rescued from tribulations is not to not be afflicted at all, but to not have been previously defeated by them, to not have been trapped by the nets of the tribulations being brought forward. 'Your hands made me and fashioned me' (Job 10:8). And this came across naturally; for so that no one might conceive of God as a brute and a necessity.

To say, through the phrase 'but who is the one being removed from your hands' [Job 5:9], the expression 'your hands made me and formed me' [Job 10:8] is brought forward, saying that even if he brings tribulations, he spares his own handiwork; for it is written: 'but he spares all, because he is merciful, O Lord, lover of souls' [Ps 145:9]. And good is the 'your hands made me and formed me', so that the 'made' is applied to the soul, while the 'formed' is applied to the body; for 'formed me' signifies the opposite, which is appropriate for the body.

And in Genesis it is said: 'God made man, according to the image of God he made him' [Gen 1:27]; for not the body is according to the image, but the soul, for God is not anthropomorphic. And elsewhere it is said: 'God formed man, dust from the earth' [Gen 2:7], taking the body, so that, as we say, we may receive the making regarding the soul, and the forming regarding the flesh. And if even the making lies regarding the flesh, it is not to be treated as strange; for to form is to make according to a kind.

But someone, speaking in opposition, says that the being formed lies regarding the soul, and this is signified from: 'He who formed [them], according to their hearts alone.' Toward which one should also wisely consider the things concerning the hands of God. And one says simply that the hands, in the plural, are the power of God's active agency; but it is also possible to take 'hand' more precisely as the Son—for it is said: 'My hand made all these things'—and the Spirit, as it is said: 'By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power' [Ps 33:6]. And it is also said: 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you, therefore the one being born in you will be called a holy Son of God' [Luke 1:35]. For so that the temple of the Savior may be established, there has been a descent of the Holy Spirit and of the power of the Most High, which is the Son.
After these things, changing, you mocked me. The creative and also the providential [aspects] of God through these [things].

english: He demonstrates, through 'your hands have made me' the creative aspect, and through 'after these things, having changed me, you have struck me' the providential aspect. For this is the work of God's providence: to surround the brave man with distress through struggle, so that he may set up a character and a goal for men, whom they become imitators of when looking toward him. But 'having changed' should be understood as 'having made a change concerning me' regarding the body; for he has struck and wounded him, being utterly desolate of all those who have been changed around him. 'Remember that you formed me of clay, and to dust you turn me back again' (Job 10:9).

Consequently, knowing Him as the Author and Lord of both creation and providence, the word turns to Him in prayer, saying: even if you have brought things upon me as if exercising authority over painful things, yet remember that I am weak and have a constitution from clay—this, however, should be understood concerning the body—and having formed me, you turn me back to dust again. And it is clear from this that he speaks concerning the body; for the soul is not turned back to dust. The things concerning the weakness of human nature proceed to exhort even friends to endurance and the knowledge of His virtue and His patience.

And now, as it is possible to fashion the body, he joined it; for fashioning is possible in type; for it is not said concerning the angels: 'He who fashioned angels,' but 'He who makes His messengers spirits.' And concerning the earth, it is said as a thick body: 'and His hands fashioned the dry land.' These things are not said to mean that God kneads with hands according to human ways, but that to each, divine discipline brings a name that is appropriate: the fashioning, as we have said, to the body, and the making to the soul. Similar to 'and to dust you turn me back again' is that which was said to Adam: 'Dust you are and to dust you shall return' (Gen 3:19).

Observe that if something is said concerning a composite, it is not necessary to understand it concerning every part. For if it is said: 'And David was meek' or 'Moses,' we do not understand this concerning his body. But if: 'And David was red with beauty of eyes,' we think this concerning his body, not concerning the soul. And here, where it is said: 'and to dust you turn me back again,' it is not necessary to calculate that this is said concerning the soul. 'Did you not curdle me like milk, and harden me like cheese?' (Job 10:10). The seed, from which [he] consists...

Regarding the living being, he says, 'as milk unmilked'; and just as milk, being curdled, becomes cheese, so also the seed, being congealed, becomes a nature. And this is the constitution before the embryo. For the seed cast into the channels of the womb, when it is curdled like cheese, becomes a nature; which moreover is spread out or, as the Scripture says, 'is imprinted' (Job 10:9) and receives [it] like a character. But when the limbs differentiate and each becomes its own and moves, for instance, like an animal's hand or foot, then the birth of the embryo clearly demonstrates the living being.

All these things, therefore, encompass, signifying through 'Remember that you formed me of clay' (Job 10:8) the creation of Adam from the beginning, and through 'You did not milk me as milk' (Job 10:10) the successive generations composed by succession. All these things, therefore, he will carry through, indicating the handiwork of God, so that through this or through prayer, one may be called to mercy.

The 'You milked' therefore, he says, showing to God, that by His energy the genuine deposition of the seeds occurs. 'Having clothed me in skin and flesh, and having placed me in bones and nerves.' This is used by those desiring to show that those whom God clothed in skin tunics, these thick things, are their bodies. For it is also said in Genesis: 'And God made skin tunics for Adam and his wife and clothed them' (Gen 3:21). But 'He made for Adam and his wife,' in order to show that He has made a garment suitable for 'male and female.'

It is clear that 'skin and flesh' here signifies the body; for he connects what follows by saying: 'and placed me in bones and nerves.' Thus he announces the whole way and the harmony of the body's constitution through those things before these and through those contained within. It should be noted that these words appear to belong to the soul; for this is the one having clothed herself, having entered into skin and flesh and bones and nerves; which signifies that she precedes the garments and the being clothed; for the subject is 'clothed.' 'And you have provided life and mercy for me, and your oversight has preserved my spirit' (Job 10:12). english: Having made me consisting of flesh and skin and bone and nerves, you clothed me, but also, 'you have practiced life and mercy toward me.' Through 'life' it signifies that the creation is placed in existence, but through 'mercy' the providential grace. For since it happens that one must also endure attacks against such a life, there is a need for mercy, as it is said: 'you have practiced life and mercy toward me.' For the Creator God does not act according to debt, but according to mercy and goodness; for it has come to be that he grants life to favorable matter rather by mercy than by any other way.

Furthermore, what follows declares more clearly the things concerning providence and its care: 'your oversight has preserved my spirit,' saying 'spirit' for the soul. For although 'spirit' signifies many things, here it signifies the soul; for if James says, 'just as the body without the spirit is dead' (James 2:26), and Stephen, encountering God and saying, 'Lord, receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59), he signifies the soul. Having these [thoughts] within yourself, I know that you are able to do all things; nothing is unable for you.

God does not possess from without those things which he is said to possess; for everything that is, being simple and existing without mixture, does not take in anything from without; for he is uncomposite. For the Creator, and the Good, and the Light, and the All—if he is rightly theologized—is these things according to his essence. And 'you are able to do all things' should be heard faithfully and prudently, so that we do not fall into the folly of the opinionated.

And what is said is clear when used by a division thus: of the powers, some are active and others are passive. The active ones are such as we perform, and the passive ones are such as we undergo, which are directed toward the activities. Therefore, if it is said that God is able to do all things, one must not attribute to him also the passive powers; for it is not possible to say that he becomes something else—for he does not possess powers according to contingency—nor is it to be said that he is able to lie, or change, or deny himself. Therefore, I say, those things are possible for God which are fitting for God. For some, including Porphyry and his like, reason in a way that if all things are possible for God, including lying, and if all things are possible for the faithful, then he is able to make a bed and to make a man. But this is not what is meant, but just as, if it is said all things are possible for the physician...

Regarding medicine, I say that all things are possible to the pilot, those things which suit his art; so if I say all things are possible to God or to the faithful, I say this: that what suits God is possible for God, and what suits the faithful is possible for the faithful. These are the things made right through faith.

For the Scripture also knows this, it says concerning God: 'If we deny, he remains faithful. For he cannot deny himself' (2 Tim 2:13). And again: 'In whom it is impossible to lie to God' (Heb 6:18). Likewise, with understanding, the 'it is not able for you' must be avoided, which can be understood by analogy with what was said in the Gospel: 'All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made' (John 1:3). Consider, then, whether it is appropriate to think so in this way: evil is a 'non-being'; indeed, those participating in it are called non-existent because of their neglect: 'For you will not deliver the scepter to those who are not.' It is also said: 'Calling things that are not as though they were,' 'that he might bring to nothing the things that are'—so that this is saying: the non-existent and evil 'is not able' for you; for it is possible to turn away from sinning.

For if I sin, 'keep me; from lawlessness you have not made me innocent' (Ps 119:117). He says this reasonably; for since I know him to be creator and provider of himself and of all things, he follows by teaching also concerning his patience. For he himself knows, according to the blessed David, that 'he does not bring wrath every day' (Ps 103:9). But God guards the one sinning, not desiring him to sin—'for he does not desire the death of the sinner as [the desire for] repentance' (Ezek 33:11)—but so that, giving the law which forbids sinning, he might cause the one practicing it to hate evil. He also rebukes the friends who suppose that he suffers through sin, teaching them that God does not give [judgment] at the same time as the sinning, so that they too might reckon this according to themselves. And he teaches the turnability of human nature through 'from lawlessness you have not made me innocent,' while also presenting a pattern of moderation and indicating the succession of Adam, showing sin to be common to men. english: Sin, which is like a stain, is caused by a corrupt upbringing; likewise, regarding the saints, one must consider a lapse as non-voluntary. Thus it has been said, 'For all have sinned' (Rom 3:23). We say that the sins of the saints are a path toward virtue.

Just as one learning to write, since he cannot write well immediately, stumbles during the learning process—not such that it is considered corrupt as if someone were writing evil by malicious intent—so also the one striving toward virtue, if he first stumbles through ignorance, is not to be punished. For if he were impious, woe to me! If he were righteous, I would not be able to bow my head. He might say, 'If I sin by choice, woe to me; but if, as we have previously stated, I have it only by succession from Adam, again I will not be able to bow my head as one completely cleansed of filth.' For of sins, those from our own choice stand as bad, but those [are different] as previously stated; for punishment follows those from choice, but purification is owed to those from ignorance. He might say, 'Even if I am righteous, I do not think greatly, knowing the obvious.' For many, having spoken highly of themselves, fell in practice.

And 'Pay attention, then, O Pharisee, speaking about God: did you not then speak truly?' (Luke 18:9); but the one who was self-important did not have the words accepted. It has been said regarding the lowly one, that 'this one descended having been justified by Him.' But I am full of dishonor. The sign of human weakness is thin, for man is full of dishonor by being a body surrounded by such a thing, about which Paul says: 'It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory' (1 Cor 15:43).

And I am hunted like a lion for slaughter. Thinking myself to be full of dishonor according to the previously stated sense, the enemy seeks to cast me down through those standing around, as if surrounding with dogs, and tries to envelop me with nets. But the lion is a great animal. It has been said: 'A lion is stronger than cattle.' 'For the righteous has become like a lion.' However, the one set out for a combatant knows that some beast is trying to hunt him; and this is the adversary, the devil. And he now calls the slip into sin a 'slaughter'; for slaughter is often said even regarding punishment. The magnitude of the assault against himself appears to exceed...

Through the saying, 'I am prowling like a lion' (Job 10:24), it is meant that the enemy is like a lion driving the wild beasts and not leaving him to avoid temptation. This is not arrogance, but it reveals the plot. For again, 'you turn me terribly' (Job 7:19). It shows that even if I prowl like a lion, so many things have surrounded me, but they do not attack by themselves; for the permission is small. If God had not permitted, the prowler would not have had the power.

The 'turning' must be understood actively as the change that happened to Job from wealth to poverty and from health to sickness; much of [text missing] has come to him. 'Renewing against me my distress' signifies the successive onslaughts of the attackers. For just as an enemy, being repelled from the opposing sides, prepares himself again to fight, the one who has taken authority devises new pains like against a man, increasing the affliction in magnitude.

This is shown by: 'while he was still speaking, another messenger came' (Job 33:23). For the calamities were frequent and successive. 'And with great wrath I used you; you brought trials upon me' (Job 7:18). And here again the magnitude of the afflictions is shown, not ceasing, but making it known to friends that this exceeding wrath is not, as one might think, because of sin, if one were to judge his life.

Anger here should not be understood as a passion, but as the attacking onslaught, just as Moses says to God: 'You sent out your wrath and consumed them like a reed' (Psalm 106:10). Some [suffer] because of sin; but here it is shown through 'you brought trials upon me' that it is not because of sins; for those being punished in this manner are not said to undergo trials. Thus, the bringing of trials must be understood not as if they had fallen upon them [by their own fault].

And this happens, which the disciples were taught in the prayer not to let happen: 'lead us not into temptation' (Matthew 6:13). Why then did you bring me out of the womb, and I did not die? And my eye did not see, and as if I did not exist, I became. Someone might think this to be out of malice, but he is turned from what was said toward God: 'But it is otherwise with you...'

english: Has it become a matter of worldly use so that you might appear righteous? He who spoke briefly is not contradicting this, saying: 'If I were impious, woe is me' (Job 3:3), but he wishes to demonstrate the bitterness of life, which a trivial man would not do; for there is pleasure in this living. Furthermore, he wants the cause to be shown clearly even to friends, through which he did not die at the same time as emerging from the womb; and it is clear that because it is destined to be, the aim is manliness.

The struggle after the flesh is also shown in another way, concerning which Paul writes: 'If we have hope in this life only, we are most to be pitied of all men' (1 Cor 15:32). And he perceives both the pleasant things of life and the bitter ones. For no one being released from the flesh finds pleasure in wealth, in debauchery, nor is he carried by the evil things. Having tested this life and the pleasant things in it—for he had become happy in many ways and was indeed rich and had health of body—having fallen from these things into their opposites, and having become experienced in these things through works, having known their vanity, he instructs us not to have desire for them by saying: 'Why then did you bring me out from the womb and I did not die, my eye not having seen, so that I might not become as one who is not?' (Job 10:1).

The vanity of the combatants in this life, such as wealth, is shown from: 'Do not fear when a man becomes rich or when the glory of his house increases, for he will not receive all things in his dying' (Prov 23:17)—for all these things do not follow the one being released from them—'for the glory of his house will not descend together with him.' For in this living, such people have trusted only. And if the saints desire, like the blessed Paul, 'having a desire to depart and to be with Christ' (Phil 1:23), to be released from life, they nevertheless accept the judgment from God. Yet the saints, quite naturally, have a desire for the body to be outside. For it is not saints alone, but also those outside the proclamation.

english: He endured by the power of God, through which he prays thankfully. Paul also says these things: 'Not I, but the grace with me' (2 Cor 12:9). He wishes to set forth 'before having gone from whence one does not return' (Job 14:6). So it is not because of himself... but because he wished to instruct his friends with these things, who indeed set forth those standing upon the trivialities as bad, and those being delivered as serious. He wished to be fully assured of the judgment concerning himself.

It is not necessary to consider that Job denies a resurrection of the dead, but rather in this way: 'from whence one does not return' (Job 14:6)... in bitter life; for he knew that he would be raised incorruptible. Into a land of darkness and gloom, into a land of eternal darkness, where there is no light and one cannot see the life of mortals. And while experiencing pains, the most manly man was preaching concerning the coming age; in this way, he was not denying a resurrection when he said, 'before I had gone from whence I do not return' (Job 14:6).

And a land of gloom and darkness of eternal darkness, where there is no light nor the life of mortals, the Saint says he first gives to himself the lesser things; for he was not saying he was in the 'kingdom of the heavens' (Matt 13:43) and in the land of your promises, O God; he happened to be among the lesser ones. Then he wishes for those who hear to be instructed concerning the judgment, that a correction of actions had not yet occurred. It should be noted that he often says the name of the earth and also a bad disposition. By this is shown the 'you have sunk into the seat' and the 'they shall enter into the lowest parts of the earth.' They called upon the... upon the earthly ones. This fits those 'bearing the image of the swine.'

It is often said that the earth is the soul, but when it has virtue, it is good, and when it is stony and thorny, it is bad. Toward those loving the pleasure in this life, he says the heavy thing: 'there is no light nor to see the life of mortals.' Having understood, Sophar the Minean says: he who speaks much and is heard, or even the eloquent man, thinks himself to be righteous. Not having the proper reverence concerning the Saint, they were more impudent or offered it to him as fitting, thinking it was for him to speak much, since they did not know the purpose of the things being announced. And speaking much is judged not from the multitude...

Regarding the words: for there is a time when... of the things... it has; but when things are said differently, which happens... with five words... [gapped]. By using an attack against him as if he were saying much, it also appears probable that 'or he who is eloquent is thought to be righteous'. For many of those committing sin, by making the words impressive through the words themselves, think they are hiding sins by the probability of the words, wanting to deceive regarding the difficulty of the things done to them; but such is not the righteous Job testifying toward God. It was not appropriate, therefore, as it was said, that they approached him because they considered the sin of the cause of the things coming upon him to be the reason; through which error... he is taunted, that even if he... the words... he is not righteous for this reason.

Blessed, a child of a woman, short-lived. He uses a probable word now, but the appropriate knowledge of the man is left behind. He says, therefore, that even if someone is eloquent and through the probability of the words brought forth by himself is thought to be righteous, he must recognize that he is short-lived. Even if someone is blessed by God and thought to be long-lived—for they thought a man blessed to be long-lasting and for many years—yet even this one is short-lived as regards the coming age; in order to show him, desiring, that he does not have precise knowledge of the things, for being short-lived according to men. And this is evident from the following things being brought forward: and 'a child of a woman' signifies the man circumspectly.

We have this said by the Lord: 'No one is greater among the children of women than John' (Matt 11:11). Graciously, the arguments for this set forth Jesus apart from the children of women through a woman because he is the Virgin; and graciously we shall say that in his [words]... 'having come from a woman' signifies here the female of the name of the woman. And in reality, the human time is short; and of this is the sign said by Paul: 'If in this life we have only hoped, we are more to be pitied than all men' (1 Cor 15:19). For this is the life of the composite man. But if [one] approaches the life coming through the intellect, he will not be short-spirited [by]...

english: For the soul is immortal. If you compare the life of Sodom, even that would be little compared to the life in the coming age and the immortality of the soul.

Do not be much in words, for the one opposing him is not [himself]. [He is] ignoring the concordant purpose of the things announced to him, and says to him: 'Do not be much in words.' And the divine word, training him not to have excess in words, says: 'From much speaking, one will not escape sin.' Here, 'much speaking' refers to the announcement that was not approaching. But the apostle makes it clear that it is not the multitude of announced words that makes it 'much speaking,' [saying] 'extending the word until midnight' (Acts 25:4) to those listening.

It is to be wondered at his audacity against Job, for even while answering him, he claimed not to be the one responding to him. Because of this, someone more audacious must be endured, [to address] him who suffers through faultiness, ignoring the other cause. For he does not say, 'I am pure in works and blameless before him.' Thinking he is advising him regarding his own assumption of purity, he approaches him as if the confession of this purity and blamelessness were a rejection of Providence; for friends think that if he had not sinned (1 Cor 11:30), he would not have fallen into dark places. But they do not show that Job said to God: 'I am blameless before you.' For he knew that 'stars are not pure before him' (Job 9:2), and what was said by those having been made righteous: 'All our righteousness is as a filthy rag before you' (Isa 64:6). For as toward you, the one being Judge (1 Cor 11:3), even if we have righteousness, we have it dim compared to you. And Paul, saying, 'I am not aware of anything against myself' (2 Cor 13:5) and adding, 'but I am not justified by this' (1 Cor 4:4), shows the weakness of natural kind.

But how would the Lord speak to you? And his lips would open with you? Since they appear to be having hesitation in speech, even if they erred regarding one thing—for it is said regarding some of them: 'Inquire of the former generation, and examine the traces of...'

The lineage of the fathers is clear: he says that he is not opening the speech of God and His lips in a human-suffering way. Therefore he says, 'Do not say, I am pure;' (Ps 51:6) but rather, make yourself fit for purity, so that in this way God might speak to you and open His lips with you through goodness. His speech and His lips are to be understood as the conversation occurring invisibly in the intellect.

For the lips manifest the word, as the proverbial saying teaches: 'The lips of the wise are perceived by insight;' (Prov 12:20) but also, 'Keep unjust lips far from you.' (Job 27:4) Furthermore, he announces to you the power of wisdom, because it shall be double to you. He makes it clear that God, speaking to you, will teach you, because He has brought these things about wisely. It is also understood that God will teach him as if regarding a just retribution; these things he was saying to Job.

It is indeed true, when God brings on pains through sin, that one capable of understanding must see the induction through His wisdom and in the bitter things, that He is not defending [the sinner], but is bringing the tribulations medically and toward the health of the soul; which one of the saints, knowing this, said: 'I will bless You, Lord, because You were angry with me for [the sake of] salvation.' To receive the knowledge of the judgments of God is a gift of God, concerning which it has been said: 'Abyss is the multitude of Your judgments.' (Ps 139:6) We know this much: that they are being accomplished toward what is beneficial, even if we do not grasp it.

And let it be as an example of an island set apart, to which the ruler sends those falling and stumbling; and it is clear that this one is to lie underneath [the rule], as everyone who is indeed sent to that island to dwell there undergoes this, even if we do not know the exact cause of the stumble. He brings a demonstration that God does all things by wisdom, saying: 'It shall be double to you'; double, as I think, meaning differing in superiority for the one who is not judged, the word being weakly advanced by him.

For because the judgments of God have deep knowledge, the blessed David teaches, to whom 'the obscure and the hidden things of wisdom' are revealed, saying: 'Your knowledge has been marveled at beyond me; it has been strengthened, I am not able toward it.' (Ps 139:6) And another says concerning wisdom: 'I said, I will act wisely, and it was removed far from me beyond what it was. And a deep depth: who will find it?' (Ps 42:9) And then you will know that it is worthy of you.

english: You have departed from the Lord because of the sins you committed (Job 1:15). He says he is still engaging in the same kind of reasoning as if speaking to one who has sinned, that if the Lord were to speak to you and make you understand according to his own wisdom, from which having known his superiority you would learn, 'that you have departed from the Lord because of the sins you committed.' And he speaks these things with presumption, not knowing the causes of those things which happen under God, toward the one being addressed, that because of manliness he endured these things, awaiting the praise from God, expecting the one who said: 'Do you intend to use me differently than that you might appear righteous?' (Job 13:28). For he himself, 'the one doing all things and transforming them,' knows the judgment of each. You will not find a trace of the Lord, nor will you reach the ends, which the Pantokrator has made.

He reasons with the holy man with a certain plausible boldness; for since he knew that the administrations of providence are great to grasp, he makes a discourse to him, saying: 'You will not find a trace of the Lord, nor will you reach the ends,' saying 'ends' in reference to the outcomes of things happening. And this one and the other friends are also rebuked; for as having grasped that he suffers these things through sin, they were running against him. But it is also possible to understand 'the ends' in another way; as it has been said: 'Bringing up clouds from the ends of the earth' (Psalm 104:2). And the end is also such a thing, for the sake of which all other things exist, but it is not for the sake of anything else. And by way of an example: the end is health; for because of this, I say, all other things, helps, and labors and efforts, are for this.

And the boundaries of the world are also called 'ends'; as it has been said: 'An infinite ocean and the worlds with it are driven by the same reins of the Master' (Psalm 104:10). The psalmist, having a concept of God as encompassing both the beginnings and the ends and altogether all things happening under him, was saying: 'Behold, You, Lord, have made all things, the ends and the ancient' (Psalm 102:18). The heaven is high, and what will you do? And what do you know of things deeper than those in Hades? Or shorter in measure than the earth or wider than the sea? He wishes to show through all these things that the knowledge of men is measured, not reaching the judgments of God. And now indeed: heaven, he says, is deeper and more distant than Hades, and the earth and the breadth of the sea; say something about them, if you are able. And he perhaps alludes to the fact that even if someone attempts concerning the earth...

They do not speak of the sea and heaven, but are ignorant of the things beyond. This can be used to refute those experienced in Greek philosophy who are said to speak of the nature of heaven, earth, or sea, when they are actually empty regarding these things and say much about Hades, claiming it is a place for souls and other things, seizing words whose demonstration they cannot make manifest; for being unparticipating in the Spirit, they do not possess the precise knowledge of these things of the holy ones who walk upon the earth and have their citizenship in heaven (Phil 3:20), so as to say: 'God has given to me unerroneous knowledge of existing things, to know the constitution of the world and the energy of the elements, the beginning, the end, and the middle of times' and the following.

But if he searches out all things, who will say to him: 'What have you done?' and this he truly says, even if he does not look toward the proper goal. 'For who resists the will of God?' (Job 41:11) It is like this: 'Does the creature say to the Creator: Why have you made me thus?' But he speaks boldly to him regarding 'if he searches out all things.' It is possible to speak regarding administration, perhaps alluding to Job, that even if he suffers, he cannot say: 'What have you done?' for it has happened justly, because we have sinned. Regardless, his perception of this is not certain. For he himself knows the works of the lawless; having seen the absurd, he will not pass them by. It is clear, then, that he spoke through the 'if he searches out all things'; for he says he knows the works of men, not being indifferent to their faults—demonstrating the unrequited justice of God—and he sees them among the foolish.

The saying is useful for the negligent. But a man is differently sounded by words, and a mortal born of woman is equal to a donkey in the wilderness. He says that those who compare the secure knowledge of God to the impositions of men are sounded in vain, comparing him to a donkey, thereby presenting the extreme slowness of men toward the apprehension of judgments, using the word excessively. For those who are accustomed to donkeys and are in the city have some experiential knowledge of the hermit from habit, and because of being naturally slow, and having the wildness and the habits of the days removed, which encourages the human race toward the knowledge of judgments. english: By personifying the ignorance of men regarding judgments, happy David says: 'Behold, these sinners, though they prosper, possess wealth for eternity (Ps 73:3-4). And I said: Therefore I justified my heart in vain, and washed my hands among the innocent (Ps 26:6), and became whipped all day long.' And after these things he says: 'I became beast-like beside You (Ps 51:16).' And the 'beside You' is good; for as regarding the knowledge of God, he says, 'I became beast-like.'

Then, in order to show that he was assuming the face of men, he says: 'But I am with You always (Matt 28:20),' indicating that: by Your participation and communion, I know. Similar to 'I became beast-like beside You' is 'But I am irrational' and 'I am earth and ash.'

For if you have nourished your heart purely, and you bow hands toward Him, if there is something lawless in your hands, make it far from you; and let injustice not entangle itself in your judgment. As if introducing an exhortation to himself as a teacher, he approaches it saying: that if even though you are exceedingly pure in this way, as always lifting up hands in prayer asking for what is from God (1 Tim 2:8), you will be well-disposed and will cast away the triviality remaining in you, but also let injustice not entangle itself in you. That is: even if it happens that you become in the beginning of doing wrong, let the wickedness not remain as entangling itself in your life.

He says these things, that moral virtue should be suitable to the purity of the soul according to understanding. Similar to this is 'lifting up hands without anger and reasoning (1 Tim 2:8).' And one is perhaps secured, thinking it possible to have a pure heart and unjust deeds. But anyone says the opposite of this, claiming it is possible to have 'just deeds and yet not' a pure heart, [is] one performing almsgiving in order to be seen by men, the practice of the heart appearing equal to the [outward] act. For thus will He take up your face just like pure water. He says, that...

Having been freed from every stain and injustice, you will have a face clean like water; it is clear he speaks of the soul. For the human, having been separated from every defilement, will truly show the 'according to the image' as pure and sincere. He will strip off filth and will not be afraid.

He moves without irregularity by the Word. For after saying 'he will lift up his face like clean water,' saying again 'he will strip off filth' is a great irregularity. However, he says this to mean that by making oneself supple toward purity, one will be freed from all filth so as to be fearless and no longer dread retribution. Likely he also says this to mean that after stripping off filth, he is fearless; for God, seeing 'the mind' and 'the hidden things,' does not punish such a person. For humans, while they are ignorant of the hidden, once they have come to know it and have received something, they are exposed and punished as having formerly sinned. But God, receiving the present virtue, forgets the former sins, just as the one who repents presents a face saying, 'Remember not our former iniquities' (Ps 103:12). And he will let the labor pass like a wave passing by and will not be tossed. He says that the labor of wounds, which they thought the holy one would suffer through sin, will be let pass and will easily pass like a wave without being tossed by it.

He says 'forgetfulness' clearly to mean not the total decay of memory, but the passing of pains; for so it has been said concerning the righteous: 'For their first tribulation shall pass upon them, and it shall not come up upon their heart' (2 Cor 4:8). 'For in the day of good things, there is an amnesty of evils' (Isa 65:17). And your prayer, like the morning star, and from midday, life rises for you. Following this, he says to those who have perished, that if you make yourself as pure that you do not even become filth, your prayer will shine like the morning star. This signifies to him that morning light, by which the brightness of virtue begins; thus the light will be as strong as its peak. Observe then, what he intends by 'life rises for you,' lest perhaps the virtue...

english: He says [it is] either the life to come or the life without toil, by transitioning from the burdensome things. And the luminous life is found being enlightened by the 'sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2). It has been said: 'In the morning I will stand by you and watch' (Ps 46:5). And it shall be certain to you that there is hope for you. And again he says that he believes from the preparation concerning the hoped-for good things.

These things indeed [are...] it is clear, that the [soul's...] follows the divine hope; for he who wishes to 'live according to God' (Acts 13:36) follows the eternal, just as Paul says: 'now faith, hope, love remain' (Gal 5:26). And from the absence of anxiety and care, peace is revealed to you. He says this, that having been freed from the burdensome and painful things through the hope having come from the preparation, 'peace is revealed to you,' saying peace as the rest from circumstances.

And we have in the divine writings things said concerning peace of the kind according to the soul, concerning which it is said: 'great peace is in those who love you, and there is no stumbling block in them' (Isa 26:3). And this, being the tranquility of the soul, is the fruit of the Spirit: 'for the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace' (Gal 5:22). From this they are blessed, concerning whom it is said: 'blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God' (Matt 5:9).

For when anyone 'casts his own care upon the Lord' (1 Pet 5:7), he shall have this peace; but the sinner shall not be in this peace, 'for all the life of the ungodly is in anxiety' (Job 21:5) being disturbed. And you shall be at rest, and he who wars against you shall not be, but many, changing [their minds], shall entreat you. Understand, if again this one says that [he] no longer is insulted as a worthless man through any kind of maltreatment; the fact that this is coming implies 'but many, changing, shall entreat you,' signifying that those who formerly rushed against you shall entreat you because of the change in you.

And the peace which is principally the tranquility of the soul is given to the holy one, the Word saying: 'every man shall rest under his vine and under his fig tree, and none shall terrify him' (Mic 4:4). And this is not sensually; but he who has the practical life, signified by the fig tree, and the contemplative, which is signified by the vine—being a poetic thing of gladness—is therefore fearless, not having a deceiver to terrify him or demons. But he who is in malice does not rest here, even in that of the thought...

Being tossed about by passions and demons. Furthermore, regarding Cain, it has been said that one ought not to be moved: 'You have sinned, be still' (Gen 4:7). For quietude of tranquility is a dwelling in human nature, whereas disorder is an intruder.

And now a symbol is interpreted as the soul dwelling in the earth: 'The earth was afraid and was still when God arose for judgment' (Ps 46:6). For when those doing earthly things become through the fear of judgment in repentance, they take up quietude instead of disturbance, hearing: 'And you will be still, without fear of every evil' (Ps 112:4), and salvation will remain for them.

It is hinted that those who fight of old are abandoned by salvation, the remnant of the righteous human being having become [lost]; and it is clear that they considered the salvation they had clothed themselves with to be the evils of those they fight against, both against soul and body. For their hope is destruction. Regarding the evil-doers, he says that expectation is destruction; he might say that their expectation is not exactly that which they themselves are expecting, but as that which follows having that [expectation]; just as we say to one falling into punishment: 'You brought these things upon yourself,' not that he himself set this forth, but that he followed it.

'But the eyes of the ungodly will be dimmed' (Ps 35:8). Perhaps he hints at the envious and their sorrow which comes upon the change of having fallen into misfortune, as he wrote. But he does not speak of these eyes—for many of the ungodly remained sharp-sighted until their later breath—but of the eyes of the soul.

You have in the divine writings concerning the eyes of man: 'The commandment of the Lord is a bright light, enlightening eyes' (Prov 6:23), meaning that God's commandments save the eyes of the inner man, even if they are blind. Having understood, Job says: 'Are you then men? Or will wisdom end with you?' (Job 9:10). He says: 'You are indeed men, but thinking great things about yourselves and regarding yourselves as the only men, you think that wisdom remains until you; but you suppose that you can grasp the judgments of God and decide something about them; and in reality, it surpasses human things.' For he says, 'Your judgments are a great abyss' (Job 9:12). But Paul also writes that these things are 'unsearchable' (Rom 11:33). And it is shown through 'will wisdom end with you?' that the wisdom of God is not [limited to] the human.

english: It is a matter of parts. The apostle knows, just as he does, that 'by a part' and for the perfect ones here 'knowledge' possesses a 'storehouse of the spirit' and these things; but he who possesses a storehouse does not have the whole of it, but a 'part' of it. But for him who 'has come to perfection,' he has the part along with the whole; for this is the storehouse.

And as for me, my heart is toward you. He wishes to present to them, saying, that they have re-formations in their own intellects, asserting: 'And my heart is toward you' and I do not agree with you in the same intellect. Or do you not think you think excessively? For I also understand; for it does not differ from the logical regarding the logical. But the difference occurs by the imposition.

He speaks, therefore, concerning faults: 'Hear me, you who have lost your heart.' For he does not speak of the essence, but of its energy, its faulty loss. For a righteous and blameless man became a reproach. When he speaks of lesser things, he applies them to himself; for he is deficient in himself through blindness. But when praise is necessary, he says of the righteous and the one possessing virtue, that they fall upon the same, just as the blessed Paul, saying, 'I know a man in Christ' (2 Cor 5:19). For God testified to him, saying, 'Do you suppose I have used you differently than that you should appear righteous?' (Job 2:9).

And if Job once said, being compelled because of the desire to glorify his friends against him, 'I know that I shall appear righteous' (Job 13:15), this became a character; he said this from the reports concerning himself of those using and working virtue, saying: 'I know that if I should use courage until the end, "I shall appear righteous."' For he did not say: 'I am righteous,' but he inclined his expectation toward a future time, announcing the proper characteristic of virtues. For he was prepared to fall at a set time, and his house was to be despoiled by the lawless. This shows that he was delivered to those who requested to test him. Some also, not using this word well, thought fate to be, referring the 'set time' to it. But this is a lie; for not every set time signifies fate. What he presents, therefore, is this: that even if he became a reproach, this did not happen unto infinity, but at the time of God's allowance for this to happen, just as...

“given into the hands of those who afflict.” He said “a fixed” “time,” which is the time for a man to use such a virtue, by which also he is called able to fight. And he says “houses” are “being shaken” regarding the virtues; for those who oppose are eager through the instigators to shake and to unsettle them; for it has been said that houses are taken instead of virtues: “because the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses.” Were they therefore homeless before they feared God? But it is clear that the virtues, according to one hearing the words of Jesus and building his own house, which is life, are not upon a sensible rock, but upon the Christ who said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church” (Matt 16:18), signifying that Peter has a house in such a rock. And the Savior builds the church, being himself both rock and builder; for God cooperates with the diligent. Thus also the psalmist says: “In a rock you lifted me up” (Ps 27:10). But it is no great gift of God to be lifted up on a sensible rock, but it is clear that it is by the secure word, as again the psalmist says: “You established my feet upon a rock” (Ps 40:2). It should be noted that [it is] the righteous or another... but the lawless.

And “to be shaken” shows the courage of the righteous having been thrown into confusion; it is also said in the psalms: “Many times they have fought against me from my youth, and indeed they were not able to prevail against me” (Ps 38:6), as also Paul: “Who shall separate us from the love of God?” (Rom 8:35) and the following. And “houses” must be understood in the plural as the abundance of virtue; temperance is a house, courage is a house, meekness and others, as it is said: “A stronghold is the holy fear of the Lord” (Ps 127:1); thus also justice. There are against these houses, which the Lord destroys: “For the Lord destroys the houses of the insolent; but he has established a boundary for the widow” (Ps 147:7). For he destroys the houses of the proud, as it is said: “Capernaum, until you ascend to heaven, shall you be brought down to Hades” (Matt 11:23), and “the one who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11). “He establishes a boundary for the widow,” which is: the house, the life of those serving God, protected from evils. And “the houses of the lawless shall undergo cleansing, but the houses of the righteous are received” also shows the lives of each.
