english: "an elder," he says, "you are, and an old one among us, becoming more weighty than even your father"—instead of "more venerable"—"knowing more than we do." And he says these things from an arrogant authority. We have "weighty" instead of "old man" written in the Royal Histories; for the purpose of showing that Eli was an old man, the text says, "and the man was weighty." This also signifies honor and abundance, as if he were saying, "I will confess to you, Lord, in a great congregation, in a weighty people, I will praise you," instead of "in honor and in abundance."

"A few of your sins have been scourged." He says this meaning: "You have sinned and because of this you undergo lashes. But since, enduring this, you add injustice to God, your sin has become more weighty." And he says these things not with understanding; for he did not know the matter as it was, so that he was speaking falsely. And there are various ways of being false. For there is a way of having lied that is not [maliciously] lying; for often we hold an opinion about something as being such and we say it, having the intention of speaking the truth, yet that which is reported is false by its own nature, but it is not said by one who is lying. And there is also the case of one who, not knowing anything at all, brings forth a false word out of arrogance, which is what happened to him.

But there are others who lie in a different way, as one who has knowledge. "You have spoken with great excess" (Job 32:2). "What did your heart dare, or what did your eyes lift up?" (Job 31:24). And they held these opinions about him, both hearing [of his sins] and because of his words of boldness. Since the blessed one brought forth words from purity, they thought this was an excess of arrogance, in vain and without understanding. "That you have broken a heart before the Lord, and have brought forth from your mouth such words." They thought [his] boldness, which exceeds [all] from purity, was anger, which happened to them from their own corrupt nature, since they had subjected themselves to blasphemy, regarding the reasonable and as it is naturally yielded, the freedom of his words, as blasphemy.

For what mortal is there that will be blameless, or that, as he is to come, will be a righteous offspring of a woman? It is a characteristic of those who do not possess virtue to consider this undertaking difficult and to place it as if no one possessed it, just as the one before says, stumbling because of the body's [nature] as it is likely [to be] weak.

If he had observed according to the soul and according to the intellect, he contemplated the greatness of human nature, which the hymnographer teaches on both sides, saying: 'What is man, that you take thought of him? Man is made like vanity' (Psalm 8:4), which he has said regarding the weakness of the body as comparing it to divine things. But instructing on greatness, he says again: 'You made him a little less than the angels, you crowned him with glory and honor' (Psalm 8:5). And again he says another saying, 'a great man' and 'a precious man, merciful,' which is not according to being born, but according to being in essence receptive of justice in the composition.

He does not believe according to the saints. Similar to this is the 'if he does not believe according to his children, he thought something crooked concerning his angels.' Thus, there he says the angels are the saints, presenting that 'if even angels are corruptible, how can a man be blameless?' It should be noted that to believe often signifies the certain, as it is said: 'All his commandments are faithful' (Psalm 146:5). And he interprets their faithfulness saying: 'established unto the age of ages.' And again: 'the word is faithful and worthy of all acceptance.' And again: 'God is faithful and there is no injustice.' For God is not faithful from participating in faith, but from having certainty. And heaven is not pure before him.

Just as even the stars will not be compared to God's light, being without any darkness, and the heaven itself is not pure, not at all, but rather in addition to God. And it is possible to call these ones who 'left the heavenly dwelling' heaven here, whom he said 'his children, concerning whom he does not believe.' For God himself says in Isaiah from his own person: 'My sword is drunken in heaven' (Isaiah 34:5). And the sword signifies punishment, as it is said: 'My sword shall eat blood of wounds, and my arrows shall be drunken with blood' (Isaiah 34:6). Thus, among the angels who have fallen, he says the sword becomes drunken, bringing punishment called heavens. Therefore, this heaven is not pure before him. And a man, being detested and unclean, drinks an equal measure of injustice. You hold [it], since you are not righteous, to whom the earth was given along with those like him, and no foreigner approaches. Thus, how he said this has been made clear. The Lord, commanding his own disciples, says: 'Do not worry about tomorrow' (Matt 6:34). And it is a command, so that 'we should throw all anxiety upon the Lord' (1 Pet 5:7). And if he also says that life is 'in care,' and that years are a numbered amount given to a ruler, then his fear is in his ears. This he says, that even if someone is a ruler and acts insolently, let him know that he has a numbered number of years.

Power does not make him long-lived; for time is measured for men by God toward His own judgment. Therefore, even if the ruler acts arrogantly, his life and his years turn out to be few, and he always has fear in his ears because of the uncertainty of the manner [of death]. Such a person has a fearful nature. For when he is in care regarding life, he reveres even death. But the diligent one, knowing that it is better 'to depart and be with Christ' (Phil 1:23), is hopeful, not being such as the wicked, but one who fears; for it has been said that 'the impious flees when no one pursues' (Prov 28:1).

When it seems to him that he is already at peace, his destruction will come. Even if someone exists in great prosperity, like the one saying in the Gospel: 'I will pull down my barns and build greater, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things, eat, drink, rejoice' (Luke 12:18-19); but the Lord says to him: 'Fool, this very night they will demand your soul from you; and what you have prepared, to whom will it belong?' (Luke 12:20). For when it seemed to him to be at peace in wealth, his destruction came.

These things, then, the divine word presents. It seems that he says these things, stumbling according to this, from the mishearings of the wise, because he was applying these to Job. Let him not believe that one turns away from darkness. The phrase 'when it seems to him to be at peace, his destruction will come' is similar to 'when they say: It is peace and security' (1 Thess 5:3). He says, 'Then, sudden destruction stands upon them just like the pangs of a woman in labor.' For he has already been committed into hands of iron, and has been arranged into pits of gypsum (Job 15:22b–23a). For the one sinning has hoarded for himself punishments, which [will come] through iron and gypsum.

english: It is signified. But there is no need to be surprised that he says such things. For it has already been said that perhaps he brings these things forward from mishearings of the ancients. He knows in himself, as in Job 15:23b, that he remains in a state of falling. He says that the conscience of those committing sin knows the expectation of the habits of the wicked, that this is a state of falling.

A day of darkness shall surround him (Job 15:23c), instead of 'he is being tossed about by afflictions.' You have in Amos concerning this day: 'Woe to those who desire the day, and why is this day of the Lord upon you? And this is darkness and not light' (Amos 5:18–20), 'and a gloom where there is no light' (Amos 5:30). This is also in Job 10:22a. Necessity and tribulation shall cast him down (Job 15:24a). He says, therefore, that the wicked will fall into these things, preparing for all [evil], because through sin he suffers these things (Job 15:24b), like a leading general falling. Even if it is not Job who is saying these things, but he possessed some knowledge of the devil, which it is likely he obtained from the words of Job or from other ancients. He calls him a leading general because of his primordial wickedness. He says, therefore, that necessity and tribulation, as mentioned in the preceding things, shall cast him down in such a way as a leading general; thus he too shall fall, being primordially wicked.

Insolence ran against him (Job 15:26a). It is manifest through the fact that he does not act in secret, but against the Lord. And insolence can be both arrogance and every injustice; for those being reproached makes them worthy of insolence. The one insulting someone says these words and calls them wicked. But he does not entirely make him worthy of insolence; for neither praise makes one good, nor reproach makes one bad. He is in the thickness of his shield. Because he is bold in evil, he shows this in this: for as he uses the shield as if invincible, through its thickness and through fleshly habits. So also the false prophets, having put on the skin of a sheep, were 'wolves snatching' from within. Concerning the devil it is said in this very book: 'Who shall uncover his face-covering, and who shall enter into the folding of his armor?' For he who uncovers his wickedness is sparse. And just as the hypocrite, having another face, shows himself to others, so also the devil...

Being transformed into an angel of light, he deceives and snatches away, and not as the devil; for if he were openly so, we would have fled him. So also the prostitute, personified in the poems, injects the venom with goodly words. But he enters into uninhabited houses.

These things seem to be said about the devil, or about every evil and opposing power and soul partaking of the same wickedness; for their receptive qualities are of the same kind. And if anything is said about the devil as evil, as a worker of evil, it is possible for this same wickedness to be said about another evil power. Therefore, in general, we say about every evil that it enters into uninhabited houses; for where there is a significant dwelling, the evil one has no place.

And we have from the Gospel to demonstrate this: 'When the unclean spirit,' he says, 'goes out from the man, it passes through dry places seeking rest and does not find it' (Matthew 12:43). But dry places in these matters are the souls that are destitute of wickedness. For often the moisture of wickedness is called water: 'So our soul has passed through the unsubstantial water.' And the devil is 'king of all those in the waters,' not of the senses—for these are works of God—but of the evils and the sinners who are caught in that water, concerning which it has been said: 'Many waters will not be able to quench the love' (Song of Solomon 8:7), instead of 'evil does not hinder love.'

Therefore, when the unclean spirit, having been cast out from the man, seeks another house, seeks where to make its den, it passes through dry places, instead of 'it does not dwell in the soul'—for it finds it destitute of the bad moistures, so that it may speak boldly in this and say: 'My soul is like a dry land' (Psalm 63:1) (and 'it does not find rest there'). The hymnist says something analogous: 'I did not know [him] when the evil one was turning away from me.'

Therefore, the souls there are 'uninhabited houses,' from which every virtue has been separated, and in the absence of which God has departed, and His word and the Holy Spirit; into which the devil, the opposing power, enters. And what those prepared, others will destroy. Having spoken about opposing powers uniquely through 'he enters into uninhabited houses,' he moves to the plural: 'What those prepared, others will destroy.' For as many as...

english: The wicked prepare for malice, while some of them, being saints, take them away from those being held by the divine proclamation, which the blessed apostles have established having been sent to 'make disciples of all nations' (Matt 28:19). And pay attention, that he did not say 'what they have done', but 'what they have prepared', and they prepared through malice, through pleasures, through other evils.

Neither shall he be enriched, nor shall his existing things remain with him. Of those prepared with diligence, how can they still be enriched? For the poor and the [gap]... [gap] prepared... [gap] of his deception... [gap] good teachers. Similar to this is 'the partridge has hatched what she did not lay; at the end of it they will leave it, at the end of it it will be a fool' (Luke 12:20). It will not cast a shadow upon the earth. Bodies are the makers of shadows, and it is impossible for a shadow to exist without a body. And this one, since having undergone a certain way, does not remain—I do not say that his essence does not remain, but that he does not remain as he wished to be—therefore he does not cast a shadow; 'for he was not from the beginning' (Job 15:13), he says, and malice 'will not be unto the age' (Job 15:35). Nor shall he escape the darkness.

And rightly so; for the one who is an instigator for others toward malice receives an irrecoverable punishment. A wind withers his sprout. Even if it seemed to flourish in those whom he deceived and in those in whom he would fulfill his malice, but this sprout is withered by the wind; for he does not have a root. For malice is not essential, but entering from without, which, when struck by temptation, which is called wind, is rebuked and falls and withers. And his flower will fall. The flower is the beginning and the precursor of fruit, and this therefore falls. Even if the one participating in malice boasts, a little later he is humbled. And this is often even beneficial, just as a physician often cuts away the tumor attached to the body with iron and does not cease to apply painful things, until he fulfills the goal, the healthy state. Let the impious, falling toward God, not consider what he thinks of himself to be secure, he says. For it will result in nothing for him. For all his action is vanity because of the [gap].

source_text: μηδὲν ὑφεστηκὸς ἔχειν. ἡ τομὴ αὐτοῦ πρὸ ὥρας φθαρήσεται. διὰ τοῦτο τὸ ἄνθος αυ᾿̣τ̣οῦ ἐκπίπτει καὶ ὁ βλαστὸς αὐτοῦ μαραίνεται, ὅτι οὐ μένει καιρὸν τελείου καρποῦ. ὅμοιον τούτῳ τὸ "μὴ γίνου σκληρός, ἵνα μὴ ἀποθάνῃς ἐν οὐ καιρῷ σου." τινὲς ἐκ τῶν τοιούτων λέξεων ταραττόμενοι εἱμαρμένην εἰσηγοῦνται καὶ λέγουσιν ὅτι «ὑπὸ καιρόν ἐσμεν ἐν οἷς πράττομεν». τὸ δὲ "πρὸ ὥρας" ἐνταῦθα «πρὸ τῆς τελεσφορήσεως» λέγει, καθὸ λέγομεν ὥραν εἶναι τρυγητοῦ ἢ ἀμήτου. οὕτω γοῦν ὁ Ἰὼβ "ἐλήλυθεν ἐν τάφῳ ὡς σῖτος ὥριμος κατὰ καιρὸν συνκομισθείς". εὐεργεσία δὲ θεοῦ 406 ἐστιν τῆς κακίας τὸν βλαστὸν πρὸ ὥρας φθαρῆναι. καὶ ὁ ῥόδαμνος αὐτοῦ οὐ πυκάσει· τρυγηθείη δὲ ὥσπερ ὄμφαξ πρὸ ὥρας, ἐκπέσοι δὲ ὡς ἄνθος ἐλαίας. οὐκ ἐπιτρέπεται εἰς τελείαν καρποφορίαν ἐλθεῖν τὸ ἄνθος αὐτοῦ. οὐδὲν δ' ἧττον καὶ τοῦτο ὡς προείρηται λυσιτελές ἐστιν καὶ χρήσιμον̣ ··ε̣λετην κακίαν εἶναι τῶν ἐν̣εργ̣ο̣ύν̣τ̣ων. τὰ δὲ τῶν δικαίων οὐχ οὕτως· τὰ γὰρ κλήματα τῆς ἀληθινῆς ἀμπέλου μένοντα ἐν τῇ συμφυίᾳ βλαστοῦσιν καὶ καρποφοροῦσιν. μαρτύριον γὰρ ἀσεβοῦς θάνατος. τὰ φθάσαντα διελθὼν τὸ πέρας τοῦ ἀσεβοῦς θάνατον ἀποφαίνεται. ἡ γὰρ τῆς κακίας τελεσιουργία θάνατον ἀπεργάζεται, οὐ τὸν κοινόν, ἀλλὰ τὸν τῆς κολάσεως. πῦρ δὲ καύσει οἴκους δωροδεκτῶν. καὶ κατὰ τὸ πρόχειρον ὠφέλειαν ἔχει, ὅτι οἱ δωροδοκοῦντες πάντως ἐπὶ ἀδικήμασι καὶ ἀσεβήμασιν τοῦτο ὑπομένουσιν. εἴρηται γάρ· "ὁ ἄρχων αἰτεῖ καὶ ὁ κριτὴς εἰρηνικοὺς λόγους ἐλάλησεν, καταθύμιον ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ ἐστιν." πῶς δὲ καίεται τοῦ δωροδέκτου ὁ οἶκος, ἐπισ̣τῆσαι δεῖ. εἴρηται· "καὶ ἐξελοῦμαι τὰ ἀγαθὰ αὐτῶν ὡς σὴς ἐκτρώγων καὶ βαδίζων ἐπὶ κανόνος ἐν ἡμέρᾳ σκοπιᾶς." ἐν γὰρ ἐξετάσει τῶν πραγμάτων ἔσται ἀπόδοσις κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον· "ὑπάγετε εἰς τὸ πῦρ τὸ αἰώνιον." ἔστιν δὲ ὅτε καὶ ἐν τῷ βίῳ τούτῳ ἡ ἀνταπόδοσις
english: Having achieved nothing, its cutting will be destroyed before its time. For this reason its flower falls and its shoot withers, because it does not remain for the time of perfect fruit. Similar to this is the saying, 'do not become hard, so that you do not die in not your time.' Some, being disturbed by such words, propose fate and say, 'we are under the time in which we act.' But 'before the time' here means 'before the bringing to completion,' just as we say a time is early or late.

Thus indeed Job says that he 'has come into a tomb like grain ripe, being gathered according to the season' (Job 29:17). And it is a blessing of God that the shoot is destroyed by wickedness before its time. And its rose will not thicken; it might be early like an eye, and it would fall like the flower of an olive. Its flower is not permitted to come to a perfect fruit-bearing. And nothing less than this, as it is foretold, is effective and useful; it is a sign of the wickedness present in those who act.

But for the righteous it is not so; for the branches of the true vine, remaining in their nature, grow and bear fruit. For the death of the impious is a testimony. Having passed through what perishes, the end appears as the death of the impious. For the working of wickedness achieves death, not the common death, but the death of punishment. And fire will burn the houses of the bribe-takers.

And according to immediate benefit it has utility, because the bribe-takers certainly undergo this upon injustices and impieties. For it has been said: 'The ruler asks, and the judge spoke peaceful words; it is the incense of his soul' (Proverbs 17:8). How then the house of the bribe-taker burns, it must be understood. It has been said: 'And I will take away their good things like a shepherd turning away and walking according to a rule in a day of scrutiny.' For in the examination of things there will be a repayment according to what is said: 'Go into the eternal fire' (Matthew 25:41). And there is when even in this life the repayment [begins].

source_text: γενήσεται κατὰ τῶν δω407 ροδεκτῶν. ἐπεὶ γὰρ "ἡ κρίσις τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν", ὅσοι διαστρέφουσιν τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ κρίματα, οὗτοι ὑπὸ κόλασιν πίπτουσιν. ἐν γαστρὶ δὲ λήμψεται ὀδύνας. τοῦτο λέγει, ὅτι πατὴρ ἔσται κακῶν γεννημάτων αἴτιος γινόμενος κολάσεων. τὰς δ' ἀμοιβὰς τὰς θείας οὐκ ἄνθρωπος γεννᾷ, ἀλλὰ θεὸς χαρίζεται· "οὐ γὰρ ἄξια τὰ παθήματα τοῦ νῦν καιροῦ πρὸς τὴν μέλλουσαν δόξαν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι εἰς ἡμᾶς." καὶ οὐ τοῦτο λέγομεν, ὅτι τῶν ἀγαθῶν ὁ σπουδαῖος οὐκ̣ ἔστιν αἴτιος, ἀλλ' ὅτι αἱ χ̣άριτες τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ αἱ δωρεαὶ ἀνυ̣π̣ε̣ρβ̣λήτῳ ὑπεροχῇ παρ' αὐτοῦ παρέχονται· "πᾶσα γ̣ὰρ δόσις ἀγαθὴ καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον ἄνωθέν ἐστιν καταβαῖνον παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς τῶν φωτῶν." ὅτι δὲ τοῖς μὲν φαύλοις ἕπεται τὰ τῆς κολάσεως τρόπον τινὰ αὑτοῖς αὐτῶν αὐτὰ ἐπαγόντων, τοῖς δὲ σπουδαίοις θεὸς ὀρέγει τὰς χάριτας, εἴρηται· "τοὺς δοξάζοντάς με δοξάσω, οι῾̣ δὲ ἐμὲ ἐξουθενοῦντες ἀτιμασθήσονται." ἡ γὰρ ἐξουθένωσις τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπιφέρει αὐτοῖς τὴν ἀτιμίαν. τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Παῦλος γράφει· "τοῖς 102 μὲν καθ' ὑπομονὴν ἔργου ἀγαθοῦ δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν ζητοῦσιν ζωὴν αἰώνιον" δίδωσιν θεός, "τοῖς δὲ ἐξ ἐριθείας καὶ ἀπειθοῦσιν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ ὀργὴ καὶ θυμὸς" ἕπεται. ἀποβήσεται δὲ αὐτῷ κενά, ἡ δὲ κοιλία αὐτοῦ ὑποίσει δόλον. πᾶσα 408 γὰρ αὐτοῦ πρᾶξις, ὡς προείρηται, ματαιότητος πεπλήρωται ἐν γαστρὶ λαμβάνοντος ὀδύνας. "συνέλαβεν γὰρ πόνον καὶ ἔτεκεν ἀδικίαν", δηλονότι τῆς κοιλίας αὐτοῦ δόλον φερούσης. δόλον δὲ ἐνταῦθα τὴν πᾶ σαν κακίαν φησίν. ἔσ̣τ̣ι̣ν̣ μ̣ὲν οὖν καὶ εἶδος κακίας ὁ δόλος, οὐδὲν δ' ἧττον καὶ πᾶσα κακία̣ καλεῖται τῷ ὀνόματι κ̣ατὰ τὸ ει᾿̣ρημένον· "ὦ πλήρης παντὸς δόλου καὶ πάσης ῥαδιουργίας" καὶ "διὸ ἀποθέμενοι πάντα δόλον καὶ ὑπόκρισιν". κοιλίαν δὲ δε̣ι῀̣ νοεῖν τὴν τὸ δ····· ··ς ψ····κα·· συνκατατ̣ι´̣θ̣ε̣τ̣αι τοῖς κακοῖς ἢ τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς. ὑπολαβὼν δὲ Ἰὼβ λέγει· ἀκήκοα τοιαῦτα
english: Judgment will come against the gifted. For since 'the judgment of God is [present]' (Rom 2:5), those who pervert the judgments of God fall under punishments. And in the belly, pains shall be taken. He says this, that [the man] becomes a father of bad-born ones, being the cause of punishments.

But the divine rewards are not produced by man, but God grants them; 'for not worthy are the sufferings of the present time to be revealed to us with the coming glory' (Rom 8:18). And we do not say this, that the diligent one is not the cause of good things, but that the graces of God and the gifts are provided through incomparable excellence from him; 'for every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights' (Jas 1:17).

Because for the wicked, the manner of punishment follows, they themselves bringing it upon themselves, but to the diligent, God directs the graces, it has been said: 'those I will glorify, but those dishonoring me shall be dishonored' (Heb 2:6). For the dishonoring of God brings upon them dishonor. This also Paul writes: 'to those who seek glory and honor through patient good work, God gives eternal life' (Rom 2:7), but 'to those from selfish ambition and who disobey the truth, wrath and anger' (Rom 1:18) follow.

And it will depart from him empty, and his belly will receive deceit. For all his practice, as it is foretold, is filled with futility, receiving pains in the belly. 'For he conceived toil and brought forth injustice' (Job 15:16), making it clear that his belly carries deceit. And deceit here he says is all manner of wickedness.

For deceit is indeed a kind of wickedness, and nothing less, and all wickedness is called by the name according to what has been said: 'O full of all deceit and all trickery' (Matt 23:28) and 'therefore laying aside all deceit and hypocrisy' (1 Pet 2:22). But the belly is to be understood as [the seat of the soul/desire], it sympathizes with the evil or with the good. Having understood, Job says: I have heard such things.

source_text: πολλά· παρακλήτορες κακῶν πάντες. δείκνυσιν διὰ τούτων, ὡς συνὼν ἀνθρώποις οἶδεν πολλὰ ἀκούσας. καὶ ἐπεὶ ἀδιαφόρως τοῖς ἐν π̣ερισ̣τ̣άσεσιν οὖσιν προσάγουσιν τὰς παρακλήσεις μετὰ τοῦ διακεῖσθαι περὶ αὐτῶν ὡς φαύλων, εἰκότως, καθὰ καὶ οἱ τρεῖς πεποιήκασιν φίλοι, ἐπήγαγεν τὸ "παρακλήτορες κακῶν πάντες" σημαίνων ἤτοι ὅτι πάντες ἀγνοίᾳ τῶν συμβαινόντων ἑτέρως ἢ ὡς δεῖ φθέγγονται ἐγείροντες μᾶλλον ἢ συστέλλοντες τὰ ἀνιαρά, ἢ τοὺς τρεῖς "πάντας" εἶπεν· καὶ γὰρ ἀπὸ τούτου τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ τὸ πλῆθος. τί γάρ; μὴ τάξις ἐστὶν ῥήμασιν πνεύ409 ματος; – – – ξατ 13 ιοβ 16,6α ἐὰν γὰρ λαλήσω, οὐκ ἀλγήσω τὸ τραῦμα. θέλει τὴν διάθεσιν αὐτοῦ τὴν γνησίαν ἐπιδείξασθαι ὅτι «ἐμοὶ μέλει τῆς ὑμετέρας σωτηρίας, ὥστε εἰ καὶ ἀλγῶ, χρῶμαι τῇ παραινέσει». εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἄλλοι ἀλγοῦντες καὶ ἀνιώμενοι ἀρκοῦνται ταῖς καθ' ἑαυτοὺς ἀνίαις, ἀλλὰ τούτῳ ἡ σωτηρία τῶν φίλων προκριτέα. ιοβ 16,6β ἐὰν δὲ καὶ σιωπήσω, τί ἔλαττον τρωθήσομαι; «εἰ δὲ καὶ σιωπῇ», φησίν, «ἐνέγκαι τὰ ὀνείδη βουληθείην, οὐ μόνον φιλοσοφίας δόξαν οὐκ ἀποίσομαι, ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον μειζόνως ὡς παράνομος κριθήσομαι τῆς σιωπῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ περὶ τὰ λεγόμενα συνειδότος γίνεσθαι νομιζομένης.» ιοβ 16,7 νῦν δὲ κατάκοπόν με πεποίηκεν, μωρόν, σεσηπότα κατ' αὐτοὺς καὶ τοῦτο λέγει φάσκων ἐκ θεοῦ τοῦτο αὐτῷ συμβεβηκέναι· οὐχ οὕτως δὲ εἶχε τὸ πρᾶγμα. εἰ γὰρ καὶ ὁ θεὸς συνεχώρησεν, ἀλλά γε οὐ προηγουμένως τοῦτο πεποίηκεν, ἀλλ' ἐξαιτησαμένου τοῦ ἀντικειμένου. "μωρὸν" δὲ ἐνταῦθα τὸ ἀναίσθητον· συνῆψε γὰρ τούτῳ τὸ "σεσηπότα". ιοβ 16,8α καὶ ἐλάβετό μου, εἰς μαρτύριον ἐγενήθη τὸ "ἐπελάβετό μου" ἀντὶ τοῦ «καθήψατο». τοῦτο δὲ εἰς μαρτύριόν μοι ἐγενήθη. καὶ γὰρ τῷ ὄντι ἡ ἀνδρεία τοῦ μακαρίου Ἰὼβ πᾶσιν ἐξάκουστος ἐξετέθη. 103
english: Many are the accusers of evils. Through these they show that, having been with men, he has heard much. And since they bring their accusations to those in distress without distinction, as if to separate them as bad ones, it is appropriate—just as the three friends have done—that he brought the phrase 'all are accusers of evils,' meaning that all, through ignorance of what is happening differently than it ought, either raise up or contract the painful things; or he said 'all' regarding the three, for from this number comes the multitude. For what? Is not the arrangement of words a matter of the spirit? [Gap] Job 16:6a: 'If I speak, I shall not lessen the wound.' He wants to show his genuine disposition, that 'I care for your salvation, so that even if I suffer, I use exhortation.' For even if others, suffering and lamenting, are satisfied with their own lamentations, by this the salvation of friends is to be preferred. Job 16:6b: 'And if I keep silent, how much less shall I be wounded?' 'And if indeed in silence,' he says, 'I were to contain the insults, I would not only fail to attain the glory of philosophy, but on the contrary, I would be judged much more unlawfully for the silence of one thought to be conscious of the things being said.' Job 16:7: 'But now he has cut me off, foolishly, having struck them' [the friends], and so says, asserting that this has happened to him from God; but the matter was not so. For even if God permitted it, He had not previously done this, but it happened because the adversary requested it. 'Foolish' here means the insensitivity; for 'having struck' is joined to this. Job 16:8a: 'And he has taken me,' and 'he has seized me' became a witness instead of 'he has cast me down.' And this became a witness for me. For in truth, the courage of the blessed Job was examined, having been heard by all.
